term:Consumer Protection.deep_dive: The body of law shielding consumers from unfair, deceptive, or abusive commercial practices — for AI, chiefly the FTC Act §5 and state UDAP statutes. Enforcement themes: AI-washing (overstated capability claims), undisclosed bots, algorithmic pricing manipulation, and dark patterns — with algorithmic disgorgement (model deletion) among the remedies.
term:Consumer Protection.exam_tip: No AI exemption exists: if a human doing it would be deceptive, an algorithm doing it is too.

term:Content Provenance (NIST AI 600-1).deep_dive: Tracking the origin and history of digital content — who or what created it, and how it's been modified — via techniques like watermarking, cryptographic signing, and metadata standards (C2PA). NIST AI 600-1 elevates it as one of four primary GAI considerations because synthetic media at scale breaks the default assumption that content reflects reality.
term:Content Provenance (NIST AI 600-1).exam_tip: Provenance of content (this one) vs. provenance of data (training-data origin) — same word, different governance layers.

term:Context of the Organization.deep_dive: ISO 42001's opening clause (inherited from Annex SL): before building an AIMS, the organization must determine its internal and external context — its role in the AI value chain, stakeholder expectations, regulatory environment, and climate. Everything downstream (scope, objectives, risk criteria) calibrates to this analysis.
term:Context of the Organization.exam_tip: Clause 4 in every Annex SL standard — context analysis precedes and shapes scope, a sequencing fact exams like.

term:Continuous Monitoring.deep_dive: The always-on watch over deployed AI: performance and error patterns, data and concept drift, fairness metrics over time, security anomalies, and usage/reliance patterns — wired to thresholds, alerts, owners, and playbooks so detection produces action. It exists because AI degrades silently: models keep answering confidently as the world moves.
term:Continuous Monitoring.exam_tip: The EU AI Act makes post-market monitoring mandatory for high-risk systems — monitoring answers are compliance answers, not just hygiene.

term:Continuous Validation.deep_dive: Extending validation past launch: periodically re-verifying that a deployed model still meets its requirements — accuracy, fairness, robustness — on current data, not the data it was born on. It closes the gap between point-in-time approval and a continuously changing world.
term:Continuous Validation.exam_tip: One-time validation at deployment is the flagged anti-pattern; 'valid then' does not mean 'valid now.'

term:Controllability.deep_dive: ISO 22989 trustworthiness property: the degree to which humans (or external agents) can intervene in a system's functioning — pause, correct, constrain, or shut down. It's the engineering substrate of human oversight: Article 14's override requirements assume controllability was designed in.
term:Controllability.exam_tip: Controllability is a system design property; human oversight is the operational practice it enables — build the first to deliver the second.

term:Convolutional Neural Network (CNN).deep_dive: The neural architecture built for grid-like data — convolutional filters slide across images learning local patterns (edges → textures → objects) with far fewer parameters than dense networks. CNNs power computer vision: image classification, medical imaging, face recognition — and thus inherit vision's governance flashpoints.
term:Convolutional Neural Network (CNN).exam_tip: Architecture-matching: CNN → images/vision; RNN/LSTM → sequences; transformer → language — three pairs worth memorizing.

term:Copyright.deep_dive: The exclusive-rights regime protecting original works of authorship — colliding with AI at input (training on protected works: fair use in the US, TDM exceptions with opt-outs in the EU), output (no US copyright without human authorship; outputs may infringe memorized works), and obligation (GPAI providers must maintain copyright policies under the AI Act).
term:Copyright.exam_tip: Two separate questions — 'can we train on it?' (contested) and 'is the output protected?' (not without human authorship) — don't let one answer bleed into the other.

term:Copyright Chapter (GPAI CoP).deep_dive: The GPAI Code of Practice chapter binding all signatory GPAI providers on copyright: maintain a copyright policy, honor machine-readable text-and-data-mining opt-outs under CDSM Article 4(3), and implement measures to prevent infringing output. It operationalizes AI Act Article 53(1)(c).
term:Copyright Chapter (GPAI CoP).exam_tip: Applies to ALL GPAI providers — only the Safety & Security chapter is limited to systemic-risk models.

term:Counterfactual Fairness.deep_dive: A causal fairness criterion: a decision is fair if it would remain the same in a counterfactual world where the individual's protected attribute differed but everything else causally consistent stayed equal. Conceptually elegant, practically demanding — it requires a causal model of how attributes influence features.
term:Counterfactual Fairness.exam_tip: Recognize it as an individual-level, causal fairness definition — contrast with group statistical metrics like demographic parity.

term:Cross-Border Data Transfer.deep_dive: Moving personal data across jurisdictions — under GDPR Chapter V, lawful only via adequacy decisions, appropriate safeguards (SCCs, BCRs), or narrow derogations, with Schrems II demanding case-by-case assessment of destination-country surveillance law. AI complicates it: training pipelines and cloud inference casually move data in ways architecture diagrams forget.
term:Cross-Border Data Transfer.exam_tip: For US transfers, think adequacy-via-Data-Privacy-Framework or SCCs plus transfer impact assessment — 'we use a US cloud' is a transfer.

term:Cross-Functional Collaboration.deep_dive: The structural requirement that AI governance decisions be made by legal, privacy, security, data science, ethics, risk, and business together — because each sees failure modes the others miss. Mechanisms: governance committees, review boards, embedded governance partners, and RACI clarity.
term:Cross-Functional Collaboration.exam_tip: Single-function answers (only legal, only IT) are systematically wrong; multidisciplinary composition is the tested principle.

term:Data Acquisition.deep_dive: Obtaining data for AI — collection, purchase, licensing, scraping, or partnership — with governance gates at the door: legal rights to each source, terms permitting the intended use, provenance recording, and quality screening. Most training-data legal problems are acquisition problems discovered too late.
term:Data Acquisition.exam_tip: Possessing data ≠ having rights to train on it — the acquisition-stage rights check is the tested control.

term:Data Annotation.deep_dive: Attaching labels to raw data so supervised learning has ground truth — often via human labelers whose guidelines, consistency, and biases directly shape model behavior. Governance touches: labeling instructions as bias vectors, inter-annotator agreement as quality metric, and labor/sub-tier considerations in outsourced annotation.
term:Data Annotation.exam_tip: Label quality caps model quality — biased or inconsistent annotation is a root cause the exam expects you to trace.

term:Data Augmentation.deep_dive: Expanding training data by transforming what exists — rotations and crops for images, paraphrases for text, synthetic minority-class examples for imbalance. It combats overfitting and representation gaps, but augmented data inherits and can amplify source biases.
term:Data Augmentation.exam_tip: A legitimate answer to insufficient or imbalanced data — but not a substitute for genuinely representative collection.

term:Data Controller.deep_dive: GDPR's accountable role: the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data. Controllers own compliance — lawful basis, transparency, data subject rights, DPIAs, processor contracts — and the label follows facts, not contracts: deciding what a model is trained for makes you a controller regardless of what the paperwork says.
term:Data Controller.exam_tip: In AI supply chains, ask who decides 'why' and 'how' — the model vendor processing on instructions is a processor; the customer deciding purposes is the controller.

term:Data Dependency.deep_dive: AI's defining reliance: system behavior is a function of the data it was trained and fed on, making data quality, representativeness, and availability first-order risk factors. Dependencies also chain — upstream source changes silently propagate into model behavior downstream.
term:Data Dependency.exam_tip: An ISO 23894 risk-source theme: when a scenario's model misbehaves, interrogate the data dependencies before the algorithm.

term:Data Drift.deep_dive: Production inputs drifting away from the training distribution — new demographics, changed formats, seasonal shifts — degrading performance even though the world's underlying input-output relationship holds. Statistical distribution monitoring catches it; retraining on current data remedies it.
term:Data Drift.exam_tip: Data drift = inputs change; concept drift = the relationship changes — pick precisely, the exam pairs them as distractors.

term:Data Governance.deep_dive: Managing data as a governed asset: lawful authority to use each source, quality dimensions measured, fitness-for-purpose verified, stewardship roles assigned, lineage recorded, and security applied across the pipeline. In AI it is the upstream half of model governance — most model failures are data failures with a delay.
term:Data Governance.exam_tip: The EU AI Act makes data governance an explicit high-risk requirement (training/validation/testing data quality and relevance) — it's law, not just practice.

term:Data Integrity.deep_dive: Assurance that data is accurate, complete, and unaltered except through authorized change — spanning accidental corruption and deliberate tampering (data poisoning being the AI-specific attack). Controls: validation checks, access restriction, versioning, checksums, and tamper-evident logging.
term:Data Integrity.exam_tip: Poisoned training data is an integrity failure with model-wide blast radius — integrity controls on training pipelines are security controls.

term:Data Lineage.deep_dive: The recorded journey of data from source through every transformation, join, filter, and feature-engineering step to the training set — the data's biography. It answers the incident question ('what fed this model?'), the audit question ('prove it'), and the rights question ('whose data is in here?').
term:Data Lineage.exam_tip: Lineage = the journey; provenance = the origin — the definitional split is a reliable test item.

term:Data Minimization.deep_dive: The GDPR principle that data must be adequate, relevant, and limited to what the purpose requires — applied to AI: fewer features, narrower collection, shorter retention, and the discipline to drop the 35 features that add nothing over the 15 that suffice. Less data means less privacy risk, smaller attack surface, and simpler models.
term:Data Minimization.exam_tip: The 50-features-but-15-perform-equally scenario has one answer: use 15 — 'more data always helps' options are bait.

term:Data Protection Impact Assessment (.deep_dive: GDPR Article 35's mandatory risk analysis for likely-high-risk processing: systematic description, necessity and proportionality assessment, risk evaluation, and mitigation measures — with supervisory-authority consultation if risk stays high. AI profiling with significant effects is a canonical trigger.
term:Data Protection Impact Assessment (.exam_tip: DPIA is legally required (personal data, GDPR); AIIA is broader best practice — scope and legal force distinguish them.

term:Data Protection Officer (DPO).deep_dive: GDPR's mandated independent advisor (Art 37-39) for public authorities and organizations with large-scale systematic monitoring or special-category processing: informs and advises, monitors compliance, advises on DPIAs, and liaises with supervisory authorities — reporting to top management, protected from dismissal for doing the job.
term:Data Protection Officer (DPO).exam_tip: The DPO advises and monitors — the controller stays accountable; making the DPO 'responsible for compliance' is a wrong-answer pattern.

term:Data Provenance.deep_dive: The origin story of data: source, collection method, date, legal terms, and consent status — recorded at acquisition because it cannot be reconstructed later. Provenance underwrites every downstream claim: lawful training data, honored licenses, defensible deletion, and credible audits.
term:Data Provenance.exam_tip: Provenance = origin; lineage = journey through transformations — paired and tested together.

term:Data Quality Review.deep_dive: The structured checkpoint assessing data against quality dimensions — accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, validity, uniqueness — before it trains anything. Reviews recur: quality decays as sources evolve, so gates belong at acquisition, pre-training, and periodically in production pipelines.
term:Data Quality Review.exam_tip: Sequencing: quality review precedes training — discovering data problems via model misbehavior means the gate was missing.

term:Data Sampling.deep_dive: Selecting a subset of data for training or analysis — where representativeness is won or lost: random, stratified, or weighted sampling each shape which populations the model actually learns. Sampling bias (convenience samples, survivorship) is a quiet root cause of downstream unfairness.
term:Data Sampling.exam_tip: When a model fails on a subgroup, interrogate the sampling frame — stratified sampling is the standard fix for imbalance.

term:Data Set.deep_dive: A structured collection of data serving a defined role in the ML lifecycle — training, validation, or test. Dataset-level governance artifacts (datasheets, version tags, quality metrics, licenses) make each set auditable; leakage between the three roles invalidates every metric computed on them.
term:Data Set.exam_tip: Train/validation/test separation is sacred — 'we tuned on the test set' scenarios are describing invalidated evaluation.

term:Data Sheet.deep_dive: Datasheets for datasets: standardized documentation covering motivation, composition, collection process, preprocessing, recommended and discouraged uses — the dataset's spec sheet, by analogy to electronic components. Paired with model cards, they form the documentation backbone of accountable AI.
term:Data Sheet.exam_tip: Datasheet documents a dataset; model card documents a model; system card documents the deployed assembly — match precisely.

term:Data Subject Access Request (DSAR).deep_dive: The exercised right of access: an individual demands their personal data plus the GDPR Article 15 metadata — purposes, categories, recipients, retention, rights, and meaningful information about automated decision-making logic. AI complicates fulfillment: data may live in training sets, feature stores, and arguably in model-encoded form.
term:Data Subject Access Request (DSAR).exam_tip: Access includes 'meaningful information about the logic' of automated decisions — not the source code, but a real explanation.

term:Data Subject Rights.deep_dive: GDPR's individual entitlements: access, rectification, erasure, restriction, portability, objection, and Article 22 protections against solely automated decisions. Each has an AI wrinkle — erasure vs. trained models, objection vs. profiling, access vs. inferred data — and honoring them requires knowing where personal data flows through the ML lifecycle.
term:Data Subject Rights.exam_tip: Rights are not absolute (erasure has exceptions; access can't violate others' rights) — but 'AI makes it impossible' is never a valid refusal.

term:Deactivation Policy.deep_dive: The predefined rulebook for turning AI systems off: triggers (risk thresholds breached, regulation changed, performance decayed, vendor sunset), authority to invoke, decommissioning procedure, data disposition, and stakeholder notice. Its existence converts retirement from emergency improvisation into a governed decision.
term:Deactivation Policy.exam_tip: Mature-practice marker: the organization decided *in advance* when and how systems die — exam scenarios reward predefined triggers.

term:Decision Tree.deep_dive: A model that splits data through a sequence of readable if-then branches to a prediction — among the most interpretable ML techniques, since the path to any decision can be traced and explained. Ensembles of trees (random forests, gradient boosting) trade that readability back for accuracy.
term:Decision Tree.exam_tip: The go-to example of interpretable ML — when a scenario demands explainability over raw accuracy, tree-based simplicity is the contrast to deep learning.

term:Decommissioning.deep_dive: The operational teardown of an AI system: executing the retirement plan — dependency wind-down, successor cutover, access and credential revocation, data return/deletion per obligations, artifact archival, and monitoring shutdown, with records preserved beyond the system's death. Verification closes it: confirming nothing still silently depends on the corpse.
term:Decommissioning.exam_tip: Records outlive the system — EU AI Act documentation retention continues after decommissioning; 'delete everything at shutdown' is wrong.

term:Deep Learning.deep_dive: Machine learning with many-layered neural networks that learn hierarchical representations — edges to shapes to faces — directly from raw data, removing hand-engineered features. It powers modern vision, speech, and language AI, and it is the paradigm that made opacity a governance problem: capability came at the cost of inspectability.
term:Deep Learning.exam_tip: Deep learning ⊂ machine learning ⊂ AI — subset questions are free points; 'deep' refers to layer count.

term:Deidentification.deep_dive: The umbrella for removing or obscuring identifiers from data — spanning weak masking through pseudonymization toward (claimed) anonymization. The operative question is always residual re-identification risk: quasi-identifiers, linkage attacks, and model memorization decide whether deidentified data is actually out of privacy-law scope.
term:Deidentification.exam_tip: Deidentified ≠ anonymous — GDPR still applies to pseudonymized data; the label matters less than the re-identification risk.

term:Deployment.deep_dive: The lifecycle transition from artifact to operation: releasing a validated system into production through a chosen strategy (canary, phased, shadow, blue-green), with monitoring live from minute one and rollback criteria pre-agreed. Governance-wise it's a formal gate: named approvers, documented go/no-go, and change management for the humans affected.
term:Deployment.exam_tip: Deployment is a decision with an audit trail, not an event — scenarios reward staged strategies and pre-defined rollback over big-bang launches.

term:Design & Construction.deep_dive: The ISO 22989 lifecycle stage where the system takes shape: architecture selection, data engineering, model building and training — the phase where governance requirements (oversight hooks, explainability, logging) must be built in, because retrofitting them later costs multiples.
term:Design & Construction.exam_tip: Cheapest risk mitigation lives here — 'address it in design' beats 'monitor for it in production' when both are options.

term:Design Defect.deep_dive: The product-liability theory that a product's design itself is unreasonably dangerous — for AI: foreseeable failure modes untested, missing safeguards, or a reasonable alternative design (more testing, human checkpoints, constrained scope) that would have prevented the harm. Strict liability means no negligence proof required.
term:Design Defect.exam_tip: Three product-liability theories: manufacturing defect (deviation from design), design defect (the design is the problem), failure to warn — map the fact pattern.

term:Deterministic Output.deep_dive: Same input, same output, every time — the property of rule-based software that AI abandons: model outputs are probabilistic, sampling-dependent, and version-sensitive. The governance consequence is that testing cannot enumerate behavior; statistical evaluation and monitoring replace exhaustive verification.
term:Deterministic Output.exam_tip: Deterministic vs. probabilistic output is why AI can't be governed like ordinary software — a first-principles contrast the exam revisits.

term:Differential Privacy.deep_dive: The mathematically rigorous PET: calibrated noise added so any single individual's presence in a dataset changes outputs by at most a provable bound (epsilon), making membership statistically deniable. Used in census statistics and privacy-preserving ML training, it trades accuracy for quantifiable privacy guarantees.
term:Differential Privacy.exam_tip: The differentiator is *provable, quantifiable* protection — when a scenario wants privacy guarantees stronger than masking, differential privacy is the term.

term:Disparate Impact.deep_dive: Discrimination without intent: a facially neutral practice — say, a hiring model's cutoff score — that disproportionately harms a protected class and can't be justified by business necessity. It's the doctrine that catches algorithmic discrimination, since models rarely 'intend' anything but routinely encode proxies.
term:Disparate Impact.exam_tip: No intent required — that is the point; disparate treatment (this term's sibling) is the intentional kind.

term:Disparate Treatment.deep_dive: Intentional discrimination: treating individuals differently because of a protected characteristic — in AI, explicitly using race, sex, or age as decision features, or deliberately targeting protected groups. Cleaner to litigate than disparate impact, rarer in algorithmic form, but not extinct: proxy use with knowledge can shade into it.
term:Disparate Treatment.exam_tip: Treatment = intentional, impact = effect-based — the pairing is one of the exam's favorite definitional splits.

term:Documentation and Reporting.deep_dive: The evidence layer of governance: contemporaneous records of decisions, tests, approvals, incidents, and changes, plus the reporting flows that keep oversight bodies informed — internal (committees, boards) and external (regulators, auditors). Its absence converts good governance into unprovable governance.
term:Documentation and Reporting.exam_tip: 'If it isn't documented, it didn't happen' — in audit and enforcement scenarios, the documented-but-imperfect program beats the perfect-but-undocumented one.

term:Downstream Harm.deep_dive: Harm materializing away from the model that caused it — a biased upstream score propagating through hiring pipelines, a hallucinated fact republished at scale, a foundation-model flaw inherited by a thousand applications. Value-chain governance exists because harm and control separate: the party best placed to prevent may be furthest from the victim.
term:Downstream Harm.exam_tip: GPAI/value-chain questions turn on this: upstream providers owe documentation and transparency precisely so downstream deployers can manage inherited risk.

term:EU AI Act.deep_dive: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the world's first comprehensive horizontal AI law: risk-tiered obligations (prohibited, high, limited, minimal), a GPAI regime, conformity infrastructure (assessments, CE marking, notified bodies), governance bodies (AI Office, Board, national authorities), GDPR-scale penalties and extraterritorial reach. It entered into force on 1 August 2024. The Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744) amended it from 27 July 2026, moving high-risk rules to 2 December 2027 (Annex III) and 2 August 2028 (Annex I).
term:EU AI Act.exam_tip: Still the most-tested instrument: know the tiers, roles and penalties cold, and learn the timeline in both its enacted and amended versions.

term:EU AI Act Penalty Tiers.deep_dive: Three fine ceilings, each 'whichever is higher': €35M or 7% of global annual turnover for prohibited-practice violations; €15M or 3% for most other obligations (including high-risk requirements); €7.5M or 1% for supplying incorrect or misleading information to authorities — with SME-proportionate caps.
term:EU AI Act Penalty Tiers.exam_tip: 35/7 → prohibitions, 15/3 → obligations, 7.5/1 → misleading info — memorize as pairs; compare with GDPR's 20/4.

term:Echo Chamber.deep_dive: The feedback loop where recommendation algorithms optimize engagement by serving more of what users already agree with, narrowing exposure and hardening beliefs. It's the canonical societal-scale AI harm: no single decision is wrong, yet the aggregate degrades discourse and autonomy.
term:Echo Chamber.exam_tip: File under societal harms with misinformation and manipulation — harms that emerge from optimization at scale, not from any single output.

term:Entry into Force (EU AI Act).deep_dive: August 1, 2024 — twenty days after Official Journal publication (July 12, 2024): the Act became law and its transition clocks started, though no substantive obligations applied yet. 'In force' and 'applicable' are different legal states, and the Act's staircase of applicability dates is measured from this anchor.
term:Entry into Force (EU AI Act).exam_tip: In force ≠ applicable — obligations arrive Feb 2025 (prohibitions), Aug 2025 (GPAI), Aug 2026 (high-risk).

term:Ethical Considerations.deep_dive: The value questions that remain after legal compliance: should we build it, who bears residual risk, is the benefit distribution just, does it respect dignity and autonomy? Governance operationalizes ethics through principles, review boards, and impact assessments — turning 'be ethical' into gates with owners.
term:Ethical Considerations.exam_tip: Legal ≠ ethical: exam scenarios include lawful-but-harmful options; governance answers weigh both.

term:Ethics by Design.deep_dive: Building ethical requirements into systems from conception — fairness constraints, oversight hooks, transparency affordances — rather than auditing them in afterward, on the pattern of privacy by design. It shifts ethics from review-stage veto to design-stage requirement, where changes are cheap and effective.
term:Ethics by Design.exam_tip: Answers embedding ethics at design consistently beat post-hoc review answers — same logic as privacy by design, generalized.

term:European AI Office.deep_dive: The Commission-housed enforcement hub for GPAI: supervises general-purpose model providers, coordinates the GPAI Code of Practice, issues guidance, and anchors Union-level consistency while national market-surveillance authorities police everything else. Created by the AI Act, operational since 2024.
term:European AI Office.exam_tip: Jurisdiction split: AI Office → GPAI models; national authorities → AI systems generally — assigning the wrong enforcer is the distractor pattern.

term:Executive Order 14110.deep_dive: The October 2023 US Executive Order on Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy AI — the Biden administration's whole-of-government AI directive: safety test reporting for powerful dual-use models (via Defense Production Act authority), NIST guidance mandates (yielding AI 600-1), agency AI governance requirements, and workstreams on privacy, equity, and workers. Revoked on 20 January 2025 by EO 14148; later US federal policy (the 2025 AI Action Plan, EO 14365 on state AI laws) points the other way.
term:Executive Order 14110.exam_tip: Know it as the origin of NIST's Generative AI Profile — and that it was revoked in January 2025, while the profile itself stays in use.

term:Expert System.deep_dive: Classic symbolic AI in production form: a knowledge base of hand-encoded rules from human experts plus an inference engine applying them — powerful in narrow domains (diagnosis, configuration), transparent by construction, brittle at the edges of coded knowledge. The historical predecessor that ML displaced.
term:Expert System.exam_tip: Rule-based, explainable, brittle — expert systems are the standard contrast case to learned, opaque, generalizing ML.

term:Explainability.deep_dive: The capacity to render a system's outputs understandable to humans — globally (how the model works) and locally (why this decision). Techniques range from inherently interpretable models to post-hoc methods (SHAP, LIME, counterfactuals). It underwrites contestability, oversight, debugging, and several legal duties (GDPR's 'meaningful information', AI Act transparency).
term:Explainability.exam_tip: Transparency = information is available; explainability = outputs can be understood — the pair is a precision-tested distinction.

term:Explainable and Interpretable.deep_dive: The NIST AI RMF trustworthiness characteristic bundling the two comprehension properties: explainable (mechanisms and outputs can be described) and interpretable (outputs are meaningful in context to users). NIST treats them as distinct but paired — a system can generate explanations nobody can actually interpret.
term:Explainable and Interpretable.exam_tip: One of the seven NIST characteristics — and NIST's subtle split (explainable = how, interpretable = meaningful why) appears in careful questions.

term:Exploding Gradient.deep_dive: A neural-network training pathology: backpropagated gradients grow uncontrollably through layers, destabilizing training entirely — the mirror image of vanishing gradients. Remedies include gradient clipping and architectural choices (LSTM gates were partly a response in sequence models).
term:Exploding Gradient.exam_tip: Training-stability vocabulary — recognize the term and its vanishing-gradient sibling; depth of math is not tested.

term:Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA).deep_dive: The look-at-your-data phase before modeling: distributions, outliers, missingness, correlations, and subgroup composition — where representation gaps and quality problems surface early enough to fix cheaply. Skipping EDA is how datasets' pathologies become models' pathologies.
term:Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA).exam_tip: EDA belongs early in the data phase — it's where the analyst first *sees* bias and quality risks the governance program must catch.

term:External Communication Plan.deep_dive: The prepared playbook for speaking about AI beyond the organization: user transparency notices, regulator communications, incident disclosures, and press response — with speakers, approval chains, and pre-cleared facts defined before a crisis compresses timelines. Improvised AI-incident messaging reliably compounds the incident.
term:External Communication Plan.exam_tip: Incident scenarios reward pre-planned communications with designated owners — 'draft a statement after containment' is table stakes, having the plan already is the answer.

term:F1 Score.deep_dive: The harmonic mean of precision and recall — a single metric balancing false positives against false negatives, favored when classes are imbalanced and accuracy would flatter a do-nothing model. Governance relevance: metric choice encodes value judgments about which errors matter.
term:F1 Score.exam_tip: Precision = of flagged, how many were right; recall = of actual positives, how many were caught; F1 balances the two — the trio travels together.

term:Face Recognition.deep_dive: Biometric identification from facial features — the governance lightning rod: GDPR special-category processing when identifying, EU AI Act prohibitions (untargeted scraping, real-time remote public identification with narrow carve-outs), Annex III high-risk classification otherwise, and demonstrated accuracy disparities across demographics.
term:Face Recognition.exam_tip: Scenario reflex: face recognition → biometric special-category analysis + AI Act tier check (prohibited? high-risk?) + bias evidence.

term:Fair Use.deep_dive: The US copyright doctrine excusing certain unauthorized uses, weighed on four factors: purpose and character (transformativeness), nature of the work, amount taken, and market effect. Whether training generative models on protected works is fair use is the defining open question of AI copyright litigation.
term:Fair Use.exam_tip: Fair use is a US doctrine and it is *unsettled* for AI training — options claiming it's clearly resolved either way are wrong.

term:Fairness.deep_dive: The principle that AI treats individuals and groups equitably — operationalized through competing mathematical definitions (parity, equalized odds, calibration) that cannot all hold simultaneously, forcing documented context-specific choices. It spans process (how decisions are made) and outcome (who gets what).
term:Fairness.exam_tip: The mature answer acknowledges metric trade-offs and picks per context with documentation — 'optimize all fairness metrics' is mathematically impossible.

term:Federated Learning.deep_dive: Training without centralizing data: the model travels to the data (devices, hospitals), local updates are computed, and only parameter updates return for aggregation. It's a PET for the collection problem — raw data never leaves — though updates themselves can leak and typically get differential-privacy or secure-aggregation reinforcement.
term:Federated Learning.exam_tip: When a scenario needs multi-party training without sharing raw data, federated learning is the named technique.

term:Feedback Loop.deep_dive: Model outputs shaping the future inputs the model learns from: predictive policing directing patrols that generate arrest data justifying more patrols; recommenders training users whose clicks retrain recommenders. Loops entrench and amplify initial bias, and they hide from static testing — only longitudinal monitoring sees them.
term:Feedback Loop.exam_tip: Feedback loops explain how a small initial bias becomes structural — cite them in scenarios where deployment data feeds retraining.

term:Feedforward Neural Network (FFNN).deep_dive: The baseline neural architecture: information flows one direction, input through hidden layers to output, no cycles or memory. The building block on which recurrent (memory) and convolutional (spatial) specializations elaborate.
term:Feedforward Neural Network (FFNN).exam_tip: Architecture taxonomy anchor: feedforward = no memory; recurrent = sequence memory; convolutional = spatial patterns.

term:Fine-Tuning.deep_dive: Adapting a pretrained model with additional domain-specific training — the economic default for LLM deployment. Governance inheritance is the catch: the fine-tuned model carries the base model's biases, memorized data, and licensing constraints, plus whatever the new data adds — and substantial modification can shift regulatory roles from deployer toward provider.
term:Fine-Tuning.exam_tip: Fine-tuning inherits base-model risk and can transfer provider obligations — two consequences in one technique.

term:Fit-for-Purpose.deep_dive: The proportionality test for data and systems: quality is not absolute but relative to the intended use — clinical decision support demands a different evidentiary bar than playlist ranking. Fit-for-purpose evaluation asks whether this data, this model, these controls suffice for this use and its stakes.
term:Fit-for-Purpose.exam_tip: Anti-perfectionism principle with teeth: the question is never 'is the data perfect' but 'is it adequate for this purpose' — proportionality is the tested logic.
